issues.description: The reported analytic sample size is inconsistent across Methods and Tables. Methods states a final sample of N = 372 after exclusions, but Table 1 and Table 2 report N = 321, and Table 3 reports N = 244. The manuscript does not reconcile these discrepancies or explain what additional exclusions reduced the sample from 372 to 321 for the main analyses. This prevents readers from understanding the actual analyzed sample and raises concerns about undocumented case deletion.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: The tables use a smaller N than the final sample reported in Methods, but no explanation is provided for the difference in the main analyses. This undermines transparency about who was analyzed and whether listwise deletion or other filters were used.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321.

issues.description: The retention counts imply 450 respondents at T4, yet the manuscript then excludes only 16 for missing time points and 78 for data quality, which would yield 374, not 372, if based on 468 T1 respondents. The arithmetic and exclusion flow are unclear, and no participant flow diagram is provided. This makes it impossible to verify the derivation of the final sample.
issues.quote: n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 ... n = 450 responded at time 4... Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample... This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: Participants who missed a wave were intentionally not invited to later waves. This design converts temporary nonresponse into permanent attrition and can induce selection bias because continued participation depends on prior response behavior, which may correlate with study variables (e.g., stress, workload, incivility). The resulting panel is not simply longitudinal attrition but administratively enforced attrition.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys).

issues.description: The attrition analysis is informal and insufficient. The authors state T1-only respondents were within one standard deviation of means and had similar demographics, but provide no statistical tests, effect sizes, or analysis of attrition at each transition. Moreover, comparing only T1-only respondents to completers ignores those dropping out later and does not establish missing completely at random or missing at random.
issues.quote: Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample of respondents who completed all four time periods – this suggests that the participants who did not complete all time periods were likely not substantially different from those included in the final sample.

issues.description: The moderation analysis loses a large portion of the sample due to missing patient acuity (N = 244 vs N = 321), yet the authors appear to use complete-case analysis without principled missing-data handling such as FIML or multiple imputation. Loss of ~24% of the main-analysis sample for moderation can materially change estimates and power, especially if missingness is associated with unmeasured factors. The claim that demographics and workplace characteristics did not differ is not sufficient to justify complete-case analysis.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: The manuscript states that the patient acuity measure had missing data but does not report how many values were missing at each wave, the total percentage missing, or whether missingness affected T1 and T2 differently. Because patient acuity is central to the moderation hypothesis, these details are necessary to judge robustness.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.description: All focal constructs, including predictor, mediators, moderator, and outcome, were assessed by self-report from the same respondents. This is especially problematic for enacted incivility toward patients, a socially undesirable behavior vulnerable to self-presentation bias. Temporal separation helps but does not eliminate shared-source bias or correlated reporting tendencies, particularly across adjacent weekly reports.
issues.quote: The study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires...

issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is operationalized via self-reported rude behavior toward patients/families. Given strong desirability and professional-norm pressures in nursing, self-reports may underreport actual behavior and may instead reflect self-criticism, guilt, or response style. The manuscript does not address validity threats specific to self-assessing mistreatment of patients.
issues.quote: Participants were asked, “Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?”

issues.description: Patient acuity is a complex clinical/workload construct, but the study operationalizes it as a single self-estimated percentage of patients considered 'severe.' This is a coarse, subjective estimate that may capture perceived workload, stress, memory bias, or department norms rather than actual acuity. The operationalization only partially matches the construct and likely varies idiosyncratically across units.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: The patient acuity item instructs respondents to rely on whatever scale their department uses, including highly heterogeneous instruments across specialties. This destroys comparability across participants because a given percentage 'severe' may mean very different things depending on the scale and unit. The inclusion of broad examples does not standardize measurement.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools”.

issues.description: The item examples include patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools as examples of patient acuity scales. PRO tools generally assess symptoms, functioning, or quality of life, not nurse workload acuity per se. This risks conceptual confusion and further weakens validity of the moderator measure.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools”.

issues.description: The negative emotions measure includes aversion, disgust, anger, and fear toward patients. Theoretical arguments center broadly on job-related negative affect, but this scale captures a narrow and potentially atypical set of patient-directed emotions, excluding common stressor-emotion responses such as frustration, irritation, sadness, anxiety, or resentment. The construct measured may therefore not align well with the broader mediator posited by the stressor-emotion model.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) aversion, (b) disgust, (c) anger, (d) fear.

issues.description: One enacted incivility item asks whether nurses 'Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility.' In many clinical interactions, patients/families may not have formal responsibility over relevant decisions, making this item conceptually awkward and potentially invalid in the nurse-patient context. The adapted content may not preserve the original scale’s meaning.
issues.quote: “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility”

issues.description: Recruitment relied on flyers at local hospitals, personal networks, social media, and online forums. This is a convenience/self-selection sample with unknown sampling frame and no response rate. Such sampling may overrepresent individuals motivated by interest in incivility, online engagement, or ties to the researchers' networks, limiting inferences about nurses generally.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies... we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks... we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states the full sampled population is unknown, making it impossible to compute a response rate or assess representativeness. This is a major reporting limitation for external validity and potential selection bias.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown

issues.description: Recruitment materials stated that participants must work full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting, but the final sample description says all participants were employed as a nurse 'part- or full-time.' This inconsistency suggests either the inclusion criteria changed or were not enforced consistently.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) ... All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time)

issues.description: The study claims to ensure participants worked in high-stakes/critical care contexts, but validation was limited and indirect. Only a randomly selected subsample of 20 participants had job titles checked against O*Net descriptors, and O*Net matching cannot verify actual unit or current duties. This weakens confidence that the sample fits the intended context.
issues.quote: In addition, we reviewed the O*Net job descriptions for a randomly selected group of n = 20 participants.

issues.description: The quantitative pilot was recruited from MTurk for a specialized population of high-stakes nurses. MTurk may not be an appropriate or reliable source for verifying occupational specialization, and the manuscript does not describe any credential checks. This matters because the pilot was used to justify scale shortening and item applicability.
issues.quote: The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.

issues.description: The authors selected the 'highest loading items' from scales to shorten measures, using pilot work and prior literature. Without preregistration or a clearly fixed item-selection plan established before main data collection, this introduces researcher degrees of freedom that can inflate reliability or favorable findings while sacrificing content validity.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability

issues.description: No preregistration, registered report, or analysis plan is mentioned despite numerous analytic decisions: shortened scales, exclusion rules, lag structure, moderator handling, and supplemental analyses. The absence of preregistration increases concern about undisclosed analytic flexibility and post hoc decision-making.
issues.quote: We tested our hypotheses using data collected across four waves separated by one-week lags.

issues.description: The confirmatory factor analysis reporting is malformed and omits the chi-square symbol and degrees-of-freedom structure in a standard interpretable way. The reported values '(269) = 862.05' and similar for alternative models are incomplete. This is a statistical reporting error that prevents proper evaluation of model fit comparisons.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than a three-factor model... (3) = 82.52... a two-factor model... (2) = 82.65... and a one-factor model (1) = 8.02

issues.description: The reported alternative CFA comparisons are internally implausible. The difference between the four-factor and three-factor models appears to be only 82.52 despite a huge absolute chi-square of 862.05, but the degrees of freedom are reported as 3, 2, and 1 for successively simpler models, which is inconsistent with standard nested CFA reporting as presented. The one-factor model value '(1) = 8.02' is especially incompatible with being worse than the four-factor model while having excellent CFI/TLI nearly identical to the focal model. This suggests serious reporting errors in CFA statistics.
issues.quote: fit the data better than a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor (3) = 82.52, RMSEA = .09, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), a two-factor model... (2) = 82.65... and a one-factor model (1) = 8.02, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98).

issues.description: The manuscript says it assessed a 'hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures' but does not specify which wave's items were used, whether item parcels were used, how repeated indicators were handled, or whether cross-loadings/residual correlations were permitted. These omissions hinder evaluation and replication of the measurement model.
issues.quote: First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures.

issues.description: Hypothesis 4's serial mediation is described with the wrong product term. For a serial path from experienced incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility, the indirect effect should multiply the path from negative emotions to compassion fatigue and the path from compassion fatigue to enacted incivility (typically a × d × b, depending on labeling). The manuscript instead states 'a × b × d' without defining path labels consistently. This indicates confusion in the mediation specification.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying each stage in the serial mediation process (a × b × d).

issues.description: The coefficient linking compassion fatigue to enacted incivility differs sharply between the narrative and tables/supplement. Table 2 shows T4 compassion fatigue -> T4 enacted incivility B = .57, whereas the supplemental OLS model reports B = .23, and Table 3 shows B = .40. Such discrepancies are not explained (e.g., different estimators, covariates, standardization), making the mediation path difficult to interpret and undermining confidence in reported effects.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57*** ... ; First, using the native lm() function in R ... compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.description: The manuscript interprets relative importance percentages as proportions of variance each predictor 'accounts for' in enacted incivility, but these percentages are decomposition shares of model R² conditional on the chosen method, not unique explained variance. Moreover, the model includes highly collinear predictors, making such shares sensitive and not straightforwardly interpretable as substantive importance. The rationale ('parameter estimate nearly six times') is also inconsistent with the coefficients subsequently reported as equal (.23 and .23).
issues.quote: Because regression only provides information on how much scores a given outcome change following a single unit change in a given predictor, we conducted a relative importance analysis to understand the proportion of variance each predictor accounts for in enacted incivility... The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.description: The supplemental relative importance analysis is motivated by the statement that the compassion fatigue parameter is 'nearly six times' that of negative emotions. However, Table 2 shows .57 versus .28 (roughly 2x, not 6x), and the subsequent OLS model reports both as .23. This contradiction suggests either a serious interpretive error or confusion between standardized and unstandardized estimates, which is not disclosed.
issues.quote: the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions... negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.description: The model uses T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility in the same regression step, undermining temporal ordering for the final mediation link. Although earlier links are lagged, this final same-wave path is contemporaneous, so the serial mediation does not fully establish temporal precedence from mediator to outcome. This weakens the longitudinal mediation claim.
issues.quote: In the second step (path d), Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue... Finally, Hypothesis 4 predicted... Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly claims mechanisms 'explain' relationships and asserts stronger causal inference from a nonexperimental self-report panel. Autoregressive models can help with temporal ordering but do not eliminate omitted-variable bias, reciprocal causation, or measurement artifacts. Statements that the method supports 'stronger causal inferences' are overstated.
issues.quote: This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects ... and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.

issues.description: The study does not adequately address plausible time-varying confounds that could simultaneously affect experienced incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility, such as unit staffing, patient volume, shift type, COVID-era conditions, supervisor support, trait negative affectivity, or coworker incivility. Work hours alone is insufficient. This limits causal interpretation of the longitudinal associations.
issues.quote: T2 Work Hours ... T3 Work Hours

issues.description: The analytic models appear to include only work hours as a substantive control beyond autoregressive terms and within-wave covariances. Key covariates relevant to both exposure and outcomes—e.g., tenure, unit type, shift, patient load, role, trait affectivity, baseline demographics—are not modeled, despite being available. This omission leaves substantial residual confounding.
issues.quote: T2 Work Hours ... T3 Work Hours

issues.description: The analytic description states that autocorrelations and within-wave covariances for all variables including controls were modeled, but the tables do not show autoregressive coefficients or all covariances. Without the full SEM specification, readers cannot tell whether key paths were estimated with appropriate lagged controls for all mediators and outcomes. This opacity is particularly problematic in longitudinal mediation, where specification strongly affects conclusions.
issues.quote: This allowed us to assess stability over time by modeling the autocorrelations (AR1) between each variable and its prior occasions and the covariances between all variables (including controls) within each wave

issues.description: The paper reports only selected unstandardized coefficients and p-values, without standardized coefficients, confidence intervals for all focal direct effects, residual variances, autoregressive coefficients, or full SEM model output. This incompleteness makes it difficult to evaluate practical importance, multicollinearity, and model adequacy.
issues.quote: As predicted and in support of Hypothesis 1, experienced patient incivility was positively related to negative emotions toward patients (B = .26, SE = .06, p < .001).

issues.description: Reliability is only indirectly shown on the table diagonal, without explicit discussion by wave or for the reduced moderation sample. Given shortened scales and repeated measurement, fuller reliability reporting and potential longitudinal measurement invariance are needed.
issues.quote: Note. N = 321. Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal.

issues.description: The study interprets changes and lagged relations across four waves, but it does not test whether the repeated measures function equivalently over time. Without longitudinal measurement invariance, wave-to-wave comparisons and autoregressive mediation may reflect changes in measurement properties rather than substantive change.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.description: Although the design temporally separates some variables, the same weekly recall period and same survey method are used for all constructs, and the final mediator/outcome path is same-wave. This limits the extent to which temporal separation reduces common-method bias or source-based inflation.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.description: A one-week retrospective report may be poorly suited to subtle, ambiguous, and potentially frequent incivility events, inviting recall bias and aggregation distortions. This is especially relevant when theorizing event-based emotional processes that may fluctuate rapidly within shifts.
issues.quote: For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.description: The manuscript frames patients and families as 'customers' and uses customer-incivility theory in a healthcare context where role expectations, power, professional ethics, and dependency differ substantially from standard service settings. While the authors acknowledge complexity, the theoretical translation is partial and may not warrant direct application of customer-service CWB assumptions to patient care interactions.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship.

issues.description: Compassion fatigue is heavily tied to exposure to others’ suffering and secondary trauma, but the proposed mechanism centers on patient incivility. The conceptual bridge from incivility-induced negative emotions to compassion fatigue is not fully established; the measured construct may reflect broader caregiving burden rather than depletion specifically caused by incivility. This weakens the specificity of the theorized serial mediation.
issues.quote: We propose that negative emotions generated due to incivility experiences may be an important reason for why repeated exposure to customer incivility may place employees at increased risk of experiencing compassion fatigue.

issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently alternates between 'customer incivility' and 'patient incivility' in tables and text. While patients are treated as customers, this switching creates ambiguity about whether measures were identical and can obscure interpretation of adapted scales.
issues.quote: Table 2 | ... Customer Incivility (T2) ... ; Hypothesis 1 predicted a positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and negative emotions towards patients.

issues.description: One major exclusion criterion concerns whether demographic information was 'reasonably consistent' across waves, but the manuscript does not define tolerance thresholds or decision rules for inconsistency. Such subjective quality control can materially affect sample composition and should be fully specified.
issues.quote: n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age

issues.description: The manuscript introduces supplemental analyses after seeing results, including conditional indirect effects and relative importance analysis. These are not clearly distinguished as exploratory in interpretation, increasing risk that post hoc findings shape conclusions without appropriate caution or multiplicity control.
issues.quote: Supplemental analyses. We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility.

issues.description: The discussion extends the findings to 'service industries' and 'customers' broadly, despite a specialized sample of mostly female nurses in high-stakes hospital contexts. The role structure, emotional labor, and patient acuity context are highly specific, making broad service-sector generalization premature.
issues.quote: Because incivility from customers is likely a common experience for employees in the service industries, providing resources that can help buffer the negative effects of experienced incivility is likely vital

issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly female and appears to exclude many non-hospital, lower-acuity, and non-nurse healthcare roles. While some of this is acknowledged, claims that the findings add to generalizability of prior customer incivility research are too strong given the narrow sample and convenience recruitment.
issues.quote: This adds to the generalizability of prior customer incivility research to further support that experiencing incivility from customers – even when the customers are patients... – is associated with detrimental employee and customer outcomes over time.

issues.description: The authors cite autoregressive controls but do not test plausible reverse paths, such as enacted incivility increasing later experienced incivility, or compassion fatigue increasing perceptions of incivility and acuity. Given theory on reciprocal incivility, omitting reverse-lag tests weakens claims about directional processes.
issues.quote: our results suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: Several correlations are extremely high (e.g., T3 negative emotions with T4 enacted incivility = .94; T3 negative emotions with T4 compassion fatigue = .96), suggesting substantial overlap among constructs or common reporting variance. Yet the manuscript treats discriminant validity as established. Such magnitudes should prompt stronger scrutiny, possibly alternative modeling, and discussion of multicollinearity and construct redundancy.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility .94

issues.description: The very high correlations among negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility suggest these may not function as distinct constructs in this dataset. Combined with self-report and weekly retrospective format, the serial mediation may largely reflect a general distress/negativity factor rather than distinct sequential processes.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility .94

issues.description: Cronbach alphas are reported as .91-.94 for 4-item incivility and negative emotion scales and .96 for compassion fatigue. While possible, such uniformly very high values, alongside extreme intercorrelations, may indicate item redundancy or response set effects. This should be discussed rather than taken as straightforward evidence of quality.
issues.quote: Cronbach’s α presented on the diagonal... T1 Customer Incivility .91 ... T1 Negative Emotions .94 ... T1 Compassion Fatigue .96 ... T1 Enacted Incivility .92

issues.description: The manuscript does not report IRB/ethics approval, consent procedures beyond recruitment materials, or data protection steps for a study involving healthcare workers discussing patient interactions. These details are standard and necessary for evaluation.
issues.quote: Participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code that was listed in recruitment materials
